title: Design a metric anomaly detection platform for 500,000 metrics
prompt:
**Interviewer:** Your company runs an online marketplace. Engineers and analysts publish about **500,000 metrics** (orders, payment errors, latency by country, ad clicks, and so on). Most arrive **every minute**; about 20% arrive hourly or daily. Today, each team sets static thresholds by hand and the on-call engineers get about **60 alerts per shift, of which fewer than 5 are useful**. Management wants a central platform that finds real incidents within **5 minutes** for key business metrics and within 30 minutes for the rest, with **at most 5 alerts per on-call person per shift**.

Design the platform: detection methods, data flow, alert logic, evaluation, scale and operations.

sections.label: Requirements & decision
sections.hint: Who gets alerts? What is an anomaly worth? Detection delay vs precision? Which metrics are critical?

sections.label: Data & features
sections.hint: Metric types, seasonality, sparse metrics, dimensions, metadata, missing data, labels from users.

sections.label: Models & baselines
sections.hint: Static thresholds, seasonal baseline + robust z, forecast residuals, model per metric type, learned model later.

sections.label: Evaluation & backtest
sections.hint: No labels at first. How do you get them? Precision, recall, delay, alerts per day, replay of past incidents.

sections.label: Serving & scale
sections.hint: Points per second, streaming vs micro-batch, partitioning, storage, cost.

sections.label: Monitoring & failure modes
sections.hint: Alert grouping, fatigue, missing data, deploys, holidays, feedback loop, monitoring the monitor.

model_answer.req:
**Users and decision.** On-call engineers decide whether to investigate or page someone. A false alert costs minutes of attention and trust; a missed incident costs revenue. The goal is **high precision for alerts that page people**, with a lower bar for 'review later' notifications.

**Targets.** Key business metrics (about 2,000 chosen with product owners): detect within 5 minutes. Other metrics: within 30 minutes. At most **5 alerts per on-call per shift**, with a target of at least **50% precision** for paging alerts. Missing data is a first-class alert.

**Tiers.** Tier 1 (critical, human-tuned thresholds on top of the model), Tier 2 (business metrics), Tier 3 (long tail, notify only in a daily digest). Different severity, different routing.

**Scope.** Detect level shifts and spikes first. Root-cause analysis (which dimension broke) is phase 2.
model_answer.data:
**Volume.** 400,000 metrics at 1-minute resolution = 400,000 points per minute = about **6,700 points/s**. Per day: 400,000 × 1,440 = **576 million points**, plus about 100,000 hourly/daily metrics. Each point is a (metric_id, timestamp, value) of roughly 16-24 bytes, so about **12 GB/day raw**, a few GB compressed.

**Metric types.** (1) smooth and seasonal (traffic, orders); (2) counters of rare events (errors); (3) ratios (conversion); (4) sparse or intermittent; (5) heavy-tailed latency (use percentiles). Each type needs a suitable method. I would classify each metric automatically (seasonality strength, share of zeros, variance) and let owners override.

**Context.** Metadata: owner, tier, dimensions (country, device). Event calendar: deploys, marketing campaigns, holidays, maintenance windows. Known events suppress or explain alerts.

**Quality.** Late and missing points. Track a *freshness* signal per metric. Use event time and allow a short lateness window before scoring.

**Labels.** None at the start. Collect: on-call 'useful / not useful' clicks, incident tickets mapped to metrics, and postmortem lists. These become the evaluation set.
model_answer.model:
**Baseline v1.** Per metric: expected value from a **seasonal baseline** (same time slot over the last 4 weeks, median, with trend adjustment) and a **robust z-score** on residuals with MAD, alert if |z| > 4 for 3 of 5 points. This works for the smooth metrics and is cheap: O(1) per point with rolling statistics.

**By metric type.** Rare-event counters: Poisson-type test over a sliding window. Ratios: test numerator and denominator volume, to avoid noisy ratios at low traffic. Latency: monitor p95/p99 per window. Sparse metrics: aggregate to a coarser grain (5 or 60 minutes) before testing.

**Forecast-based option.** For high-value seasonal metrics fit a model with holidays and trend (STL + ETS or a global boosting model with calendar features) and alert when actual leaves the 99% prediction interval. Use it where simple baselines fail.

**Then ML.** After 3 to 6 months of labels, train a supervised ranker on features (z-score, duration, size, metric tier, past alert precision) that scores alerts, to decide who gets paged. Keep the z-score as a transparent feature.

**Do not start with deep learning.** It is harder to debug and the labels are not there yet.
model_answer.eval:
**Offline replay.** Take 6 to 12 months of history and a list of known incidents (postmortems, tickets). Replay the detector exactly as in production (point-in-time, no future data). Measure **recall of incidents** and **detection delay**. Count alerts per metric-day to estimate **alert volume**.

**Precision.** Sample 200 alerts and have engineers label them. Use the on-call feedback labels after launch. Report precision at each tier.

**Synthetic injection.** Add spikes, dips and level shifts of known size into real series to measure sensitivity per metric type: 'what is the smallest 20% drop we catch within 5 minutes?'.

**Business criteria.** Alerts per on-call per shift ≤ 5, share of incidents found by the platform before a human or customer report, mean time to detect.

**Do not report accuracy.** Anomalies are rare, so a detector that says 'normal' is 99.9% accurate.

**Rollout.** Run in shadow mode for 4 weeks next to the old static thresholds, compare, then migrate tier by tier.
model_answer.serve:
**Architecture.** Metrics are sent to a **message queue** (partitioned by metric id). A **stream processor** keeps per-metric state (rolling window and seasonal profile) and scores each new point. Points are also written to a **time-series store** (hot: 30 days at 1-minute; cold: aggregated).

**Compute.** 6,700 points/s with an O(1) update per point is tiny: one machine could do it in principle, but we run about 20 partitions for fault tolerance and growth. State size: per metric 4 weeks × 1,440 minutes would be 40,000 values, too big. Keep a **seasonal profile at 5-minute slots × 7 days = 2,016 values per metric** (~16 KB) × 500,000 = about **8 GB of state**, fits in memory across the cluster. Profiles are rebuilt by a nightly batch job.

**Alert path.** Detector output goes to an alert service: persistence rule, dedupe, grouping (by service, deploy id or correlated metrics), severity, routing, cooldown. Latency budget: ingestion 1 min + scoring < 1 min + persistence of 3 points = about 5 min for key metrics (use 1-minute data and 2-of-3 persistence for tier 1).

**Reliability.** Idempotent state updates, checkpointing, replay from the queue after a crash. If the model service fails, fall back to static thresholds. Backfill of a fixed profile is a batch job, safe to rerun.

**Cost.** Mostly storage and the stream cluster. Track cost per million points.
model_answer.monitor:
**Alert quality.** Dashboards of alerts per team per shift, precision from feedback, time to acknowledge, mute rate. A rising mute rate means the detector is too sensitive.

**Grouping and root cause.** Use topology and correlation: if 200 metrics of one service break after a deploy at 14:02, send one alert with the deploy, top affected metrics and dimensions.

**Known events.** Deploys, campaigns and holidays are inputs. Black Friday looks like an anomaly to a 4-week baseline, so mark known events and learn yearly seasonality for key metrics.

**Failure modes.** (1) Slow drift gets absorbed into the baseline: add a long-window comparison. (2) A long outage becomes 'normal' after a few days: freeze the baseline during an open incident. (3) Low-traffic hours make ratios noisy. (4) Delayed data causes false dips: wait for the lateness window. (5) Seasonal profile errors after DST changes. (6) Feedback bias: engineers only click on alerts they see.

**Monitor the monitor.** Heartbeat metrics and synthetic anomalies injected every day to prove the pipeline works; freshness alert on the platform itself; on-call for the platform.

**Improvement loop.** Weekly review of false positives and missed incidents, threshold tuning per tier, retrain the ranker monthly.

rubric.item: States the success criteria in numbers: detection delay, alerts per on-call, precision target
Separates metric tiers and metric types and chooses a method per type
Proposes a seasonal baseline with robust statistics (median/MAD) as the first detector
Explains how to get labels and evaluate: incident replay, synthetic injection, on-call feedback
Sizes the data volume, state and compute with numbers
Describes alert logic: persistence, grouping, dedupe, severity, cooldown
Treats missing/late data as a first-class problem
Handles known events (deploys, holidays) and baseline contamination during incidents
Monitors the platform itself and has a fallback
Avoids starting with deep learning; has a staged path to ML with labels

follow_ups: A metric has a level shift after a product change and it is permanent. How does the platform stop alerting and learn the new normal?
An engineer says 'you missed the payment outage'. How do you investigate and prevent it?
How do you detect an anomaly in a ratio such as conversion rate when traffic is low at night?
How would you find which dimension (country, device, version) caused a drop in total orders?
How would you handle 20 million metrics instead of 500,000?
Customers ask for a 'sensitivity' slider per metric. How do you build it and what could go wrong?
